📷 Photographer — $50–$90/hr
Remote | Contract | Video Annotation | Data Labeling | Photography | Visual Quality
10000 openings

Required Skills: Video annotation | Data labeling | Attention to detail | Spotting visual details in footage | Photography knowledge applied to judging images | Following rules the same way every time

Role Title: Photographer
Role Type: Contractor
Location: Northern America, Latin America, Europe, UK, Oceania.

Photographers are sought to contribute their expertise to a video annotation project. In this role, you'll apply your expertise to help train next-generation AI systems. Your work will shape how models learn, reason, and perform through high-quality, real-world input. No prior experience in AI is required — your domain knowledge is what matters.

Scope of Work
• Review video footage of robotic arms performing a variety of tasks, ensuring careful observation of each session.
• Apply detailed video annotation and data labeling skills to tag and categorize footage according to specific grading guidelines provided by the project.
• Evaluate visual and photographic quality within the videos, applying photography principles to judge image clarity, composition, and relevance.
• Spot and document visual nuances, discrepancies, or issues in robot task execution, maintaining strict attention to detail at all times.
• Follow established project protocols and grading rules consistently for all assigned sessions to ensure exceptional data uniformity and reliability.
• Submit clear, accurate annotations and written observations through project tools and workflows.
• Collaborate asynchronously with trainers and project coordinators as needed to clarify guidelines or improve annotation quality.

Preferred Qualifications
• Professional background in photography, with a keen eye for visual composition and technical image evaluation.
• Demonstrated experience in video annotation, data labeling, or related AI training projects, ideally involving robotics or technical footage.
• Exceptional attention to detail and an ability to spot subtle visual cues in dynamic environments.
• Strong adherence to complex guidelines and repetitive processes without sacrificing accuracy or quality.
• Experience using annotation platforms or visual data tools is highly desirable.
• Comfort working independently and managing deliverables in a remote, asynchronous project setting.
• Background knowledge in machine learning, robotics, or AI annotation projects is a plus but not required.

7 Direct Threats to the Indian BPO Industry

The Indian BPO industry is entering a phase where traditional cost and manpower advantages may no longer be enough.

1. AI & Automation replacing traditional BPO processes
Impact: Lower headcount requirements, reduced transaction-based billing, and pressure on traditional outsourcing models.

2. Global economic slowdown & cautious client spending
Impact: Lower revenues, delayed expansion, hiring freezes, pricing pressure, and margin compression.

3. Geopolitical conflicts & global trade disruptions
Impact: Cost escalation, currency volatility, delayed client decisions, and business-continuity risks.

4. Cybersecurity threats & customer data breaches
Impact: Financial penalties, higher compliance costs, reputational damage, and potential client attrition.

5. Competition from GCCs & alternative outsourcing destinations
Impact: Greater competition for deals, pricing pressure, and the need to demonstrate measurable business value beyond labor arbitrage.

6. Rising operating costs & shrinking margins
Impact: Greater productivity pressure, workforce optimization, site consolidation, and difficult cost decisions.

7. Stricter client expectations & evolving quality models
Impact: Higher service-level expectations, contract penalties, increased rework, and potential loss of business.

My perspective on the biggest structural change

The biggest long-term challenge may not be a global recession or geopolitical conflict.

It is the transformation from a manpower-based outsourcing model to a technology-enabled, outcome-based service model.

For BPO leaders, the future will require more than people management. It will require strong capabilities in:

• Operational excellence
• Process redesign
• AI & automation governance
• Quality analytics
• Digital transformation
• Outcome-based delivery

The question is no longer simply: “How efficiently can we manage people?”

It is increasingly becoming:

“How effectively can we combine people, technology and intelligence to deliver measurable business outcomes?”

That shift could define the next phase of the Indian BPO industry.

I think a lot of people in software are going through some version of this.

Your contract expires, or you get laid off, and when you start looking for the next job you realize the industry you knew has changed underneath you. All the time you spent learning the technology and business around your previous work suddenly feels less valuable. You wonder whether you should have spent more of that time on AI, because now AI seems to be becoming a requirement for staying employable.

Maybe you have been programming for decades. You have seen technologies come and go before, but this feels different. You are also older now, and while you see decades of experience, some hiring managers may see someone who could be resistant to change.

So you keep applying, but at the same time you dive as deeply into AI as you can. Not because it is just another interesting technology to learn, but because this time it feels existential. I know this because I am living some version of it right now.

You start projects, experiment, and look for problems other people may have missed. Partly because you want to learn, partly because you want to prove that you can still build something relevant, and partly because after working for most of your adult life you have forgotten how not to work. The empty space is uncomfortable. Working on technical problems gives you purpose and keeps the bigger worries quiet for a while.

Your family believes in you, but sometimes you can see the worry creeping in. You talk about ideas, architectures, models, agents, research, things you would normally discuss with colleagues. They listen because they care about you, even when much of what you are saying is difficult to follow. And you realize they are carrying some of this uncertainty too.

You worry about the next job, where the industry is going, and whether the projects you are putting so much energy into will become some of the countless projects that never get finished, never get used, or never get noticed. So you put that worry back into the work and keep going. When other people depend on you, giving up does not feel like an option.

Then you open LinkedIn and realize everyone seems to be processing the same uncertainty in public. AI adoption is too fast. AI adoption is too slow. AI will replace us. AI will make us more productive. Coding is dead. Coding has never been more exciting. Everyone wants confirmation that they understood what is happening correctly.

I am not sure anyone really knows yet.

We are living through a very strange transition in software. There is enormous opportunity, but also enormous uncertainty, and behind all these arguments are real people trying to figure out whether they still have a place in the industry while their families quietly live through that uncertainty with them.

It is a strange time. Be kind.

An 89% union vote in Calgary. A bipartisan letter to the FCC. And 10,000 new contact center jobs in Metro Manila.

All in the same week.

WestJet's Calgary contact center staff voted 89% to join Unifor — two years after roughly 400 of their colleagues' roles moved to agents in El Salvador. Days later, a Democrat from Arizona and a Republican from West Virginia co-signed a letter asking the FCC to force call centers to disclose which country an agent is sitting in, plus guarantee callers a right to reach a human when AI is running the call.

Don't read this as a threat to Philippine outsourcing. Read it as a change in the rules of the game.

The work isn't disappearing. TP is hiring for 10,000+ roles across Mega Manila right now — telecom, healthcare, financial services, travel. 60,000 employees here after 30 years.

The work is relocating. And the politics is a response to the direction of travel, not the volume.

What actually shifts for anyone running delivery here:

Offshoring just stopped being purely an economics story and became an organized one. A unionized client-side center means the next transition gets negotiated differently — slower, more publicly, with a press release written by someone who isn't you.

Country disclosure, if it passes, turns delivery location from a contractual line item into a consumer-facing fact. Buyers will start asking how you handle that. The smart ones already are.

Then there's the quiet part. Novo Nordisk cut 13,000 roles in a year — and 4,000 of those never showed up in a restructuring announcement at all. They just didn't replace people. Most headcount leaves a large employer this way, invisible to every layoff tracker. The displacement numbers everyone quotes are understating real movement.

Meanwhile, four in 10 workers now believe quitting and rejoining beats staying for a raise — up from 18% two years ago. And U.S. job openings, hires, quits and layoffs are all flat.

Nobody's moving. When exit stops working, voice is what's left. That's the thread connecting all of it.

The Philippines isn't watching this from the sidelines. It's the market these policies are being written about. The providers who treat country disclosure, workforce stability, and retention economics as operational problems to solve — not PR problems to manage — will be the ones still winning contracts in 2027.

The rest will be reacting to someone else's press release.

Legal conference season is in full swing, and AI has been part of nearly every conversation. 

My takeaway from LegalOps.com's Running Legal Like a Business in Vegas, Buying Legal Council's NYC conference and the conversations I had at the Pro Bono Partnership annual gala: AI is increasing the amount of work an in-house team can keep in-house. Before hiring another lawyer, it’s worth looking at the workflows behind the request (What keeps coming up? What’s going outside? What does it cost?)

AI of course speeds up repeatable work (making it easier to bring in-house) -- things like contract review, pulling terms from large document sets, initial research, drafting. Lawyers still need to use judgment on advice, exceptions and business decisions. Firms remain important when a matter calls for specific expertise in high-stakes matters.

After practicing litigation and spending more than 20 years working with in-house teams, I see the opportunity is, increasingly, matching the work with the right legal provider and technology. At Axiom, we compare the cost of a human doing the work without AI vs. a human using AI while considering different tools for different workflows. 

Based on this past conference season, teams are defining what additional work they can bring in-house. The next question is what they’ll do with the time they gain: take on more work? spend more time on complex matters? something else? ...maybe we'll have answers by next conference season.

The 2026 State of Data Engineering report surveyed over 1,000 practitioners, and the signal is clear: the era of the generalist data engineer is closing. The most advanced teams are no longer optimizing for throughput; they are optimizing for survivability under agentic AI workloads.

The non-obvious shift I am seeing in production is that the rise of AI-assisted pipeline development is creating a new bottleneck. Tools now generate 80% of the boilerplate transformation code, but they also introduce subtle semantic drift. The teams that are winning are not the ones that adopt AI fastest; they are the ones that embed semantic validation gates at every stage of the pipeline. If a generated transformation produces a schema that does not match the data contract, the pipeline should reject it at the planning stage, not at runtime.

Another pattern that is under-discussed is the platformization of data management. The trend toward centralized data platforms is accelerating, but the hidden cost is the loss of domain-specific optimization. The most effective architecture I have observed is a hybrid: a shared platform for storage, governance, and cost-control, with domain-specific teams owning their own compute and transformation logic. This prevents the platform team from becoming a bottleneck while still enforcing cross-cutting policies like data lineage and access control.

The third structural change is the maturation of data pipelines designed specifically for AI applications. These are not traditional ETL jobs with a machine learning model bolted on at the end. They are continuous, bidirectional flows where the output of inference directly triggers data ingestion or transformation rules. I have seen this pattern reduce feature engineering cycles from weeks to hours, but it requires a fundamentally different approach to schema design and error handling. You cannot use a dead-letter queue when the pipeline is self-modifying.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to maintain legacy Airflow DAGs or tune Spark shuffle partitions. I am seeking a problem where I can design the governance and validation frameworks that make AI-assisted data engineering reliable at scale. If your team is struggling with semantic drift from AI-generated code, platformization that creates new silos, or building pipelines that react to model outputs in real-time, I want to hear about the specific workload patterns and compliance requirements you are facing.

What is the one data engineering bottleneck that, if solved, would allow your team to safely double the velocity of AI-augmented pipeline development?

Employers aren't cutting people, but they aren't adding them either. Every open req now has to justify itself. Hiring managers want a near-perfect fit — without a six-month search.

What we see from the staffing side
Cautious companies still have critical gaps: a senior engineer, a data lead, an AI specialist. They just won't carry the cost or risk of a slow, wrong hire.

1. Hire for the specific outcome, not the generic title.
2. Verify skills before the offer, not after the first quarter.
3. Stay flexible. Contract-to-hire and nearshore teams in your time zone add capacity without locking in fixed headcount.

A freeze is when disciplined hiring pays off most. The companies that keep building through it will be far ahead when hiring picks back up.

Every Narrative Bent contract is 30 days at a time, and month 1 is always about strategy. A client can take the plan and walk. Here's why I sell it that way.

An engagement with us starts with a month of strategy. We pull market data, talk to the client's customers, audit the technical foundation and how AI assistants describe the brand, and come back with a plan and an editorial calendar. 

Then the client decides. 

They can hand the plan to their in-house team, take it to another agency, or start production with us in month 2. Either way they've paid for the strategy and they own it.

After that it's 30 days at a time. 

No annual contract and no penalty for leaving. I set it up this way for 3 reasons:

1. long contracts hide bad work. 
If a client can leave next month, we have to earn next month, and that's the only accountability I trust

2. the buyers we work with, heads of growth and marketing at real estate and finance companies, won't sign anything longer anyway. Fighting that wastes everyone's time

3. a plan the client owns gets executed. A plan that only lives in an agency's deck gets forgotten the day the retainer ends

The downside is obvious. 

Revenue is less predictable, and I've had clients use the 30-day out. However, most of them stick around. Our typical engagement has run 9 months or more, because the work has to hold up every month.

If you're hiring an agency and they won't let you buy the strategy on its own, ask what they're worried you'll find out.

How FAST do you need someone? 
-If the answer is "yesterday," contingent staffing can get a skilled person in the seat while you hire for the long term.

Do you NEED a local, or just the right skills? 
-Sometimes the best fit is right here in Vegas.

The jobs report this morning was a flashing red warning light and my mortgage and real estate feed responded with, "Yay, rates are coming down! Now's the time to buy!"

As a former MLO, I understand the urge to cheer, but- having been a recruiter and a career coach in the non-mortgage world- it feels like a gut punch because I'm also immersed in a lot of the actual anxiety-fraught conversations with the unemployed, underemployed and those scared about losing their jobs.

A lower rate does very little if...

☢️ You are afraid your job may disappear. 
☢️Your commissions, bonus, contract work, or overtime have dried up.
☢️ You were laid off and took a lower-paying role. 
☢️You are employed but working fewer hours than you need. 
☢️You've spent 6-12 months searching and have drained the savings that would have been your down payment.  
☢️You don't trust that a new job, a promotion, or a relocation is stable enough to support a 30-year obligation. 

Back in February I wrote that lower mortgage rates would not unlock the housing market if buyers did not feel secure in their jobs and incomes. 

Today's numbers are why I'm revisiting it. 

🔻 Historically, a healthy labor market adds 150,000 to 200,000 a month, and the 12-month average is 45,000. September only added 29,000 jobs against a forecast of roughly 84,000.  Health care supplied about 17,000 of those jobs, and every other major industry changed little.  The fact that healthcare keeps propping up the rest of the industries masks stagnation elsewhere. 

🔻July and August were revised down by a combined 60,000 (July was a net loss). 

🔻Unemployment rose to 4.2%, wages are up just 3.0% over the past year. 

🔻1.9 million Americans have been unemployed for 27 weeks or longer, more than a quarter of everyone out of work.  

🔻The average unemployed American has been looking for work for about six months.  

🔻On top of that, 4.5 million people are underemployed, working part time because they can't find full-time work. 

The one bright spot is that we've added 100's of thousands of AI-related jobs since 2023 (data annotators, data center workers) and there's been a data center construction boom. BUT, a data center takes lots of people to build but very few to run, so that hiring ends when construction does. AI is also already taking over work humans used to do, and the AI bubble could burst, taking the building boom with it. 

All this doesn't bode well when we're talking about a pipeline of new buyers or even refi borrowers. 

Housing runs on stable employment, durable income, household confidence, savings, and the willingness to take a 30-year risk. Rates touch only one of those. 

Lower rates may open the door a little. Stable jobs and incomes are what let people walk through it.

✅ Cost optimization initiatives

✅ Economic and market uncertainty

🔹 Continuous learning

🔹 Technical upskilling

🔹 Building professional networks

🔹 Staying adaptable in a rapidly changing marketplace

As someone who closely follows workforce trends, I believe these layoffs reflect a larger story than one company's restructuring.

We're seeing employers become increasingly selective with hiring while continuing to evaluate organizational costs and productivity. The labor market isn't in crisis, but caution is clearly growing across multiple sectors.

Behind every layoff statistic is a person, a family, and a career transition. Those realities should remain at the center of every workforce decision.
